title: The Maureen Ponderosa Wedding Massacre

jokes.text: Episode cold open: screaming, chaos, running in darkness before any context is given
jokes.setup: Episode begins with terrified screaming and desperate calls for each other with zero context
jokes.punchline: The audience has no idea what's happening, creating comic dread before the story is explained
jokes.explanation: Classic in medias res cold open that works for Always Sunny — drops you into mayhem. The chaos is funny because it's so committed and unexplained. Rewatch bonus because knowing what happens makes the screaming funnier.

dialogue.line: God!

jokes.text: Detective: 'I got a groom -- face is half gone!'
jokes.setup: Detective is listing casualties from the wedding as though reading a routine report
jokes.punchline: 'Face is half gone' delivered with bureaucratic matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of a gruesome detail as though it's paperwork is very effective. 'Face is half gone' is specific and vivid enough to get a real laugh. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Detective
dialogue.line: Those are some interesting marks on your neck. Let me guess. Ex-wife's getting remarried, you get a little jealous.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm tired of paying alimony.' / Gang: 'Well, we got your back, bro.'
jokes.setup: Dennis explains the entire reason he wants the wedding to happen is purely financial self-interest
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately frames his mercenary motivation as friendship loyalty ('We got your back, bro')
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny character comedy — the gang's complete inability to perceive Dennis's selfishness as selfishness, just treating it as a valid reason for group action.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why is Maureen getting married in the middle of the woods?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's a monster day.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Three people crashing a wedding — it's gonna make a scene. Why couldn't you just let me do this alone?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is upset the gang tagged along
jokes.punchline: The irony that ONE person crashing a wedding is somehow fine in his logic but three is a scene
jokes.explanation: Solid character-specific logic gap — Dennis's obliviousness about what constitutes 'making a scene' is very on-brand. Not a huge laugh but consistent character work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Just don't like getting bussed up there. I feel like we're gonna be trapped.

jokes.text: 'Why is Maureen getting married in the middle of the woods?' / 'Some people find the woods romantic, I guess.'
jokes.setup: Completely valid question about an objectively strange wedding venue
jokes.punchline: Mac's shrug of an answer — delivered as genuine wisdom — is the joke. He has no idea either.
jokes.explanation: Functional exchange that gets a mild chuckle. Mac's earnest non-answer is mildly amusing but not special.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm tired of paying alimony.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Just don't like getting bussed up there. I feel like we're gonna be trapped.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains his reluctance to attend
jokes.punchline: His instinct is entirely correct — they do get trapped — delivered with no self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Better on rewatch because Mac's anxiety is completely validated. Functions as foreshadowing that becomes retroactively funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You know why? 'Cause it's Friday the 13th.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'You know why there's bats everywhere? 'Cause it's Friday the 13th.'
jokes.setup: Characters notice bats in the woods on the way to the wedding
jokes.punchline: Charlie attributes the presence of bats in the woods entirely to the date, not the habitat
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie-specific logic — ignoring the obvious (woods have bats) in favor of superstitious magical thinking. High character integration score because only Charlie believes this. Also pays off later when bat biting becomes a plot point.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Jesus Christ! You guys crashing my wedding? Wait. What?! You?! Wait, Liam, you're marrying Maureen?

jokes.text: Liam McPoyle reveals he's the groom. 'Big-time. Don't be jelly.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks 'you're marrying Maureen?' with shock — this is completely unexpected
jokes.punchline: Liam responds with the smuggest possible swagger: 'Big-time. Don't be jelly.'
jokes.explanation: The McPoyles are recurring absurdist villains and Liam delivering casual teen-speak bravado ('Don't be jelly') in this context is a perfect character note. Unexpected word choice for this character, great economy. One of the episode's stronger pure laugh moments.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: Big-time. Don't be jelly.

jokes.text: Dennis asks about Ryan McPoyle; Liam says 'Ryan's dead to me. He's dead!' / Dennis: 'So I take it he doesn't approve?'
jokes.setup: Liam dramatically declares Ryan is 'dead to me' with enormous emotional emphasis
jokes.punchline: Dennis's completely flat 'So, I take it he doesn't approve?' deflates the drama perfectly
jokes.explanation: Classic straight-man deadpan that works beautifully. Liam's melodrama is punctured by Dennis's bureaucratic understatement. The structure is clean and the economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: Oldest angle in the book, my friend. Love.

jokes.text: Liam: 'That's a negative, Ronald McDonald.'
jokes.setup: Dennis asks what Ryan thinks about the marriage
jokes.punchline: Liam responds with 'That's a negative, Ronald McDonald' — a completely random, inexplicable insult nickname for Dennis
jokes.explanation: The randomness is the joke — Liam has no reason to call Dennis 'Ronald McDonald' and it perfectly encapsulates the McPoyles' bizarre internal logic. Short, punchy, memorable. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: That's a negative, Ronald McDonald.

jokes.text: Liam: 'See you bitches on the dance floor.'
jokes.setup: Liam has just been confrontational and weird, now he needs to exit
jokes.punchline: He exits with casual, street-level swagger that is completely at odds with his character and the situation
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical button on the Liam scene. The incongruity of this weird, insular clan member saying 'See you bitches on the dance floor' is a great character-specific absurdist laugh. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: See you bitches on the dance floor.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he heard someone wanted to ruin the wedding — cut to: Frank, sitting there looking guilty
jokes.setup: Mac says there were people there to ruin the wedding, implying outsiders
jokes.punchline: The camera reveals it's Frank — one of their own group — who was the threat
jokes.explanation: Solid structural beat — the reveal that the saboteur was sitting with them the whole time is a good comedic twist delivered efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm here to support my friend, Bill Ponderosa. I'm his AA sponsor!

jokes.text: Frank: 'That is bullshit! I was there to support my buddy. That was a swervy road.'
jokes.setup: Frank is accused of trying to ruin the wedding
jokes.punchline: His defense is 'that was a swervy road' — a completely non-sequitur, implausible denial
jokes.explanation: Very Frank — his denial is so incoherent and irrelevant it becomes its own joke. 'Swervy road' as an alibi is the kind of non-logic Frank specializes in.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I just got tagged by a bat!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He got you.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I got tagged!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Suck out the poison, Dee!

jokes.text: Frank claims to be Bill Ponderosa's AA sponsor
jokes.setup: Frank announces he's attending as Bill's AA sponsor — implying a supportive, sober role
jokes.punchline: Frank is demonstrably the least qualified person alive to be anyone's sobriety sponsor
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in character — Frank as an AA sponsor is an inherently absurd concept that pays off immediately in the following scene. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Let's go break up this wedding.

jokes.text: Charlie gets tagged by a bat. 'Suck out the poison, Dee!' / Dee: 'I'm not sucking on your head.'
jokes.setup: Charlie gets hit by a bat and immediately demands Dee suck the venom out of his head
jokes.punchline: Dee flatly refuses with 'I'm not sucking on your head' — a completely reasonable response to an insane request
jokes.explanation: Solid escalating chaos beat. Dee's refusal is the sane response to an insane situation. Rewatch bonus because this bat bite is the entire engine of the episode's plot (it's what 'infects' Dee with bat rabies in their mythology).

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'll give you $200, you suck it out.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: $200? I'll do it!

jokes.text: Frank: 'I'll give you $200, you suck it out.' / Dee: '$200? I'll do it!'
jokes.setup: Dee just said she won't suck Charlie's head wound
jokes.punchline: Frank offers $200 and Dee immediately, eagerly agrees — revealing her refusal was entirely about price
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of Dee's principled refusal. The speed and enthusiasm of '$200? I'll do it!' is what makes it land — it reveals that she has no actual objection, just a price point. Excellent structure and character integration. Dee's mercenary self-degradation is core to her character.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Did you swallow it?!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Of course I swallowed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Make yourself throw up!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Suck it harder!' while Dennis yells 'This is the kind of thing I was talking about!'
jokes.setup: Dee is sucking the 'poison' from Charlie's bat wound on his head
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest 'Suck it harder!' over Dennis's legitimate complaint creates layered absurdity
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Charlie's sincere urgency with the inherent double entendre works. Dennis being exasperated by the whole thing adds another layer. Not the sharpest joke but physically funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Let's go break up this wedding.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Stop, stop! So you were there to break up the wedding. Shit. Did I just say that part?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'There is no poison from a bat!' — revealing the entire gross scene was pointless
jokes.setup: Dee has just sucked on Charlie's head wound for pay; everyone is yelling about vomiting the poison
jokes.punchline: Dennis calmly states the medically obvious fact: bats aren't venomous, the whole thing was for nothing
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the disgusting escalating sequence was based on a false premise is perfectly timed. The chaos, the money, the sucking — all for nothing. The calm correction in the middle of frantic yelling is a great structural choice. Rewatch bonus because this sets up the bat rabies subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: The McPoyle bloodline's been pure and clean for a thousand years. This marriage is an abomination.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Did you swallow it?!' Frank: 'Of course I swallowed.'
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to vomit up the bat blood he just sucked from Charlie's head
jokes.punchline: 'Of course I swallowed' — delivered with complete matter-of-factness about an objectively disgusting act
jokes.explanation: Frank's total unselfconsciousness about disgusting behavior is very on-brand. The declarative 'Of course I swallowed' implies this is normal behavior for him.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: The McPoyle bloodline's been pure and clean for a thousand years.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: When you say 'pure and clean,' you mean what, exactly?

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Means we haven't bred outside the bloodline.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Deandra. Let's go break up this wedding.' / Dennis: 'Whoa, stop, stop!'
jokes.setup: Frank has been loudly insisting he's only there to support Bill
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to 'Let's go break up this wedding' the moment Dennis is distracted — his cover story abandoned in seconds
jokes.explanation: Quick callback that reveals Frank's total insincerity. The speed of the pivot — no hesitation whatsoever — is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: For a thousand years?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. That makes a lot of sense.

jokes.text: Detective interrogation: 'Did I just say that part?' after accidentally confessing
jokes.setup: Dee accidentally reveals Frank said 'Let's go break up this wedding' in front of police
jokes.punchline: She immediately asks 'Did I just say that part?' — as if she might be able to un-confess
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom self-incrimination beat but executed cleanly. 'Did I just say that part?' is a good line — the awareness of the mistake combined with the hope it can be walked back.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Okay, I brought a disguise.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Meh! They're gonna know who you are.

jokes.text: Pappy McPoyle: 'The McPoyle bloodline's been pure and clean for a thousand years. This marriage is an abomination.'
jokes.setup: An ancient McPoyle elder appears to explain why the wedding must be stopped
jokes.punchline: 'Pure and clean for a thousand years' as a defense of an incestuous bloodline
jokes.explanation: The McPoyles' long-established incest joke pays off with Pappy framing inbreeding as racial/familial purity. Dark, specific, and deeply character-integrated. The elder McPoyle as a figure of authority arguing for incest is a great escalation of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: Now sneak me in so we can go kill Maureen.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Kill? Who said anything about killing anybody?

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Means we haven't bred outside the bloodline. For a thousand years?' / Dennis: 'Yeah.' / Charlie: 'That makes a lot of sense.'
jokes.setup: Pappy explains the McPoyles haven't bred outside the bloodline for a thousand years
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely sincere 'That makes a lot of sense' — he has no idea this is horrifying
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sincere agreement with an argument for incest is perfectly on-brand — he's not evil, just completely disconnected from normal social reasoning. 'That makes a lot of sense' said with genuine conviction about a thousand-year inbreeding program is a great Charlie moment.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Well, I feel it would be best if I pounded a beer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'll support that decision.

jokes.text: Pappy: 'Dennis knows Maureen better than anyone. Only he can talk her out of this.' / Dennis: 'The last thing Dennis wants is to break up this wedding.' / Frank & Dee: 'But we do.'
jokes.setup: Pappy explains his plan — have Dennis stop the wedding
jokes.punchline: Dennis refuses; Frank and Dee immediately volunteer themselves with cheerful enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition works well — Dennis has a legitimate reason to want the wedding, while Frank and Dee's motivations are purely to torment Dennis. Clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: You're my sponsor, Frank. Come on. My support system.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Right, right, right. Of course. So, do whatever you feel is best.

jokes.text: Mac's disguise — 'Meh!' — the gang immediately says 'They're gonna know who you are.'
jokes.setup: Mac announces he has a disguise and dramatically reveals it
jokes.punchline: The disguise is transparently inadequate; everyone immediately says it won't work
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac delusion beat. The confidence he has in an obviously inadequate disguise is very Mac. Without seeing it the joke is somewhat lost in transcript form but the reaction confirms it's visually funny.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Well, I feel it would be best if I pounded a beer.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'll support that decision.

jokes.text: Pappy: 'Now sneak me in so we can go kill Maureen.' / Gang: 'Kill?!'
jokes.setup: Pappy has been making a reasonable-sounding (if deranged) case about bloodline purity
jokes.punchline: He casually adds 'kill Maureen' as the logical endpoint, to everyone's horror
jokes.explanation: The casual escalation to murder as a solution is perfectly constructed — Pappy treats it as obvious next step and the gang's shocked 'Kill?!' reaction is the contrast. Great economy and dark subversive tone.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: I mean, it's a dry wedding, for God's sakes. They're serving milk.

jokes.text: Bill Ponderosa: 'Oh God Frank, I am not gonna make it. I am itching to get blitzed.' / Frank: 'Why are you telling me this?' / Bill: 'You're my sponsor, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Bill approaches his sponsor (Frank) in a moment of sobriety crisis
jokes.punchline: Frank has completely forgotten he's supposed to be a sponsor — 'Why are you telling me this?' — suggesting zero investment in the role
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff for the sponsor joke. Frank's 'Why are you telling me this?' reveals he wasn't even pretending internally — he genuinely forgot his own cover story. Great character work.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: I feel like maybe I should do some drugs then, you know?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That bad? You earned it.

jokes.text: Frank's AA sponsorship: Bill says he wants to pound a beer. Frank: 'I'll support that decision.' Bill: 'It's a dry wedding, they're serving milk.' Frank: 'I feel like maybe I should do some drugs then.' Frank: 'You earned it.'
jokes.setup: Bill asks his sponsor for support in resisting the temptation to drink
jokes.punchline: Frank enthusiastically endorses every bad decision — beer, then drugs — as a 'sponsor'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best extended comedic sequence. Frank as the world's worst AA sponsor is perfectly constructed — each step escalates the irresponsibility. 'You earned it' in response to 'I feel like maybe I should do some drugs' is the perfect Frank line. The structure escalates through beer → dry wedding → drugs, with Frank endorsing each step. 'You're a good person' as the sponsor's affirmation before recommending drug use is exceptional character comedy. Very high character integration — this could only be Frank.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're a bad sponsor.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Why? I supported every decision he wanted to make.

jokes.text: Mac to Charlie: 'You're a bad sponsor.' Frank: 'Why? I supported every decision he wanted to make.'
jokes.setup: Mac points out Frank is a terrible sponsor
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely sincere defense: he gave full support to every destructive choice
jokes.explanation: Frank's self-defense is impeccable — he genuinely believes 'supporting every decision' is what a sponsor does. The logic is internally consistent and completely wrong. Very high character integration. Great button on the whole sponsor sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, are you thinking what I'm thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah. We could definitely get laid here.

jokes.text: Mac to Charlie: 'Dude, are you thinking what I'm thinking?' Charlie: 'Yeah.' Mac: 'We could definitely get laid here.' Charlie: 'Huh? What?'
jokes.setup: Mac sets up a 'thinking the same thing' moment, implying tactical planning about the chaos
jokes.punchline: He's thinking about getting laid at this nightmare wedding; Charlie wasn't thinking that at all
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup. Mac's obliviousness to the chaos around him in favor of sexual optimism is very Mac. Charlie's 'Huh? What?' shows they weren't on the same page at all. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, I realize my timing is a little unorthodox, but, I figure what better way to make sure your union is totally complete than by having you sign these documents that I need you to sign?

jokes.text: Dennis to Maureen: 'I figure what better way to make sure your union is totally complete than by having you sign these documents that I need you to sign?'
jokes.setup: Dennis claims to be there to ensure Maureen's happiness on her wedding day
jokes.punchline: His 'caring' speech is entirely about getting her signature on legal documents he needs — barely disguised selfishness
jokes.explanation: Solid Dennis character beat — his 'caring' framing barely conceals his real motive. The verbal gymnastics of 'documents that I need you to sign' betrays him. Consistent Dennis selfishness humor.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You big, giant new titties, Maureen! Why would you do that now? Why not when we were together when I could've...?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'My Maureen, you've... you've enhanced yourself.' / Maureen: 'Yeah, I got my tooth fixed.' / Dennis: 'I'm talking about your tits!'
jokes.setup: Dennis is taken aback seeing Maureen; his 'enhanced' comment seems euphemistic and thoughtful
jokes.punchline: Maureen assumes he means her tooth; Dennis explodes — he means her new breast implants
jokes.explanation: Great misdirection — 'enhanced yourself' could be many things; Maureen's sweet answer (tooth) makes Dennis's explosion funnier. The specificity of 'You big, giant new titties, Maureen!' is a great Dennis line — inappropriate, specific, and self-centered. High impact.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm talking about your tits! You big, giant new titties, Maureen! Why would you do that now? Why not when we were together when I could've...?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Why would you do that now? Why not when we were together when I could've...?' / 'Why weren't you more clear with me, Maureen?'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just seen Maureen's new implants
jokes.punchline: He blames her for not getting implants while they were married — when he 'could have' benefited — and accuses her of not being 'clear' that she would change physically
jokes.explanation: Peak Dennis sociopathy. His complaint that Maureen changed herself after the divorce — depriving him of the 'improved' version — is exactly the kind of narcissistic grievance that makes Dennis funny and terrifying. 'Why weren't you more clear with me' as a genuine complaint about her not signaling future plastic surgery is an outstanding character moment. Very high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What is that all about?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'll tell you what that's all about. Zombies.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie discussing Pappy McPoyle's strange behavior — 'Zombies.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie look at the increasingly strange McPoyle behavior and try to explain it
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate, confident diagnosis: 'Zombies'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's confident incorrect diagnosis is very on-brand. 'Zombies' as a one-word response to social awkwardness is funny. Rewatch bonus because we know it's bath salts.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Once one gets a taste for its own kind, it can spread through the pack like a wildfire. Mindlessly chomping and biting at their own hinds.

jokes.text: McPoyle elder: 'The McPoyles sprung from my loins, fully formed! One of them babies tried to eat me! I ate him first!'
jokes.setup: Pappy is raving about the McPoyle bloodline amid the chaos
jokes.punchline: 'One of them babies tried to eat me! I ate him first!' — a matter-of-fact claim of cannibalism of his own infant
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. The escalation from 'one of them babies tried to eat me' (already absurd) to 'I ate him first' is shockingly dark and perfectly economical. The matter-of-fact delivery implied by the structure — no apology, no explanation, completely natural — is the key. High originality because the specific claim of preemptive infant cannibalism as a point of pride is genuinely unexpected. This is the kind of dark absurdism Always Sunny does at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You know the thing about a rat? It's got life in its eyes. Black eyes like a doll's eye.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I'm with Charlie. I'm leaving.' / Dennis: 'You guys are just gonna leave?!'
jokes.setup: Pappy has just said he ate his own baby; chaos is escalating
jokes.punchline: Mac's decision to leave is delivered with casual finality as though this is a totally proportionate response
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat. The decision to flee is entirely reasonable given what just happened, which makes it a mild comedy of manners — the gang's self-preservation instinct versus Dennis's obsession with the signature.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are you doing the speech from Jaws? Are you doing Jaws? We don't have time for this shit.

jokes.text: Pappy McPoyle's genealogy of the McPoyle bloodline: 'Syphilis killed about half of us. Mongoloidism got most of the rest.'
jokes.setup: Pappy describes how the McPoyle bloodline — 'pure as the driven snow' — has fared over the centuries
jokes.punchline: The result of their purity: syphilis killed half and 'Mongoloidism' got the rest — a perfect dark punchline on inbreeding consequences
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark comedy construction. The setup ('pure as the driven snow') is delivered with enormous pride, then the two-part punchline systematically destroys the idea of McPoyle superiority with the actual consequences of inbreeding. The structure is elegant: build up pride, then deflate with disease and birth defects listed as casually as weather. The 'Mm' and 'Right' and 'Yep' reactions from the listener add to the deadpan horror. Among the episode's best craft.

dialogue.speaker: Pappy McPoyle
dialogue.line: The McPoyles sprung from my loins, fully formed! One of them babies tried to eat me! I ate him first!

jokes.text: Dee announces she's leaving. 'I'm gonna go.' / Everyone begs her to stay / 'And we never saw Dee again.' 'Oh, no.' / 'No. We saw Dee.'
jokes.setup: Dee tries to leave, the others beg her to stay, and there's a dramatic 'we never saw her again' narration
jokes.punchline: Immediately corrected: 'We saw Dee.' — the false drama deflated instantly
jokes.explanation: Good meta-narrative joke about the retrospective framing device. The false dramatic narration punctured immediately by 'No. We saw Dee.' is a clean structure.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: Syphilis killed about half of us. Mongoloidism got most of the rest.

jokes.text: Gang shouting at Dee not to go down: 'We just got attacked by a bunch of zombies!' / 'A zombie must have stolen your car!' / 'There's no way out of here!'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to leave and the gang warns her not to
jokes.punchline: 'A zombie must have stolen your car' — the casual attribution of car theft to a zombie, as if this is the logical conclusion, is an absurd escalation of their panic spiral
jokes.explanation: The zombie-stole-your-car logic is funny in context — it escalates reasonable panic into completely unreasonable conclusions. Solid absurdist moment.

dialogue.line: Syphilis killed about half of us. Mongoloidism got most of the rest.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie: 'She's infected! She's infected!' after seeing Dee acting wild
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie have been convinced there are zombies; Dee returns acting erratically
jokes.punchline: They immediately apply their zombie theory to Dee's behavior
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff. The zombie theory being applied to Dee is satisfying because we can see (from transcript context) she's acting erratically for real reasons. The gap between their explanation and reality is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And we never saw Dee again.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We saw Dee. Yeah.

jokes.text: Ryan McPoyle declares: 'It's time we move on. Liam convinced me it's not our blood that's being tainted. It's us tainting the blood of others. McPoyles will take over the world!'
jokes.setup: Frank's plan was to have Ryan talk Liam out of the wedding; instead Ryan has been converted
jokes.punchline: Ryan now shares Liam's vision of McPoyle world domination through strategic outbreeding
jokes.explanation: Great reversal — the person sent to stop the wedding has joined the cause. 'McPoyles will take over the world!' as the conclusion of their weird genetic logic is both funny and escalates the McPoyle mythology perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: She's infected!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She's infected!

jokes.text: Frank: 'Goddamn it! It backfired!'
jokes.setup: Frank's scheme to ruin the wedding via McPoyle sibling rivalry has failed
jokes.punchline: 'It backfired!' — delivered with genuine shock and offense, as if he expected better from his terrible plan
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction line. Frank's genuine surprise at his plan failing is funny but not exceptional. The delivery would carry more than the writing here.

dialogue.speaker: Ryan
dialogue.line: It's not our blood that's being tainted. It's us tainting the blood of others. McPoyles will take over the world!

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie debate zombie vs. vampire vs. Batman logic after the bat bite
jokes.setup: Mac theorizes that Dee sucking bat poison turned her into a zombie
jokes.punchline: Mac correctly notes 'you're mixing up your horror genres' — a vampire bat would make you a vampire, not a zombie — leading to Batman being raised as a third option
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly sharp comedy. Mac's pedantic 'you're mixing up your horror genres' is a funny self-aware moment, then the conversation devolves into whether Batman counts ('He just likes bats'). The specificity of the genre taxonomy argument and the genuine logic they're applying to absurd premises is very Always Sunny. 'A grown man who dresses up like a bat and goes around solving crimes and mysteries' as a straight description of Batman is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Remember when Dee, you know, she sucked that bat poison or whatever out of Frank's head from the vampire bat?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why would a vampire bat turn you into a zombie? You're mixing up your horror genres.

jokes.text: Mac: 'He just likes bats. That can't possibly be what Batman's about.' / Charlie: 'It's about a grown man who dresses up like a bat? And goes around solving crimes and mysteries, yes. These are Academy Award winning movies.'
jokes.setup: Mac refuses to believe Batman is just a guy who likes bats
jokes.punchline: Charlie's earnest defense of Batman as serious cinema ('These are Academy Award winning movies. This is serious stuff.') while simultaneously proving Mac's point
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest film-crit defense of Batman ('Academy Award winning movies') while simultaneously describing it as 'a grown man who dresses up like a bat' is a great character moment. Very Charlie — he has film opinions that are both wrong and right simultaneously. 'Sometimes [the Academy] is atrocious' from Mac is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You're mixing up your horror genres. If anything, it would turn you into a vampire. Right or a bat, or a bat. Or Batman.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Well, you know the Academy, Charlie, I mean... sometimes it's atrocious.'
jokes.setup: Charlie invokes the Academy Awards to defend Batman's legitimacy
jokes.punchline: Mac concedes the Academy point with 'sometimes it's atrocious' — treating film criticism as a shared concern while zombies attack outside
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Batman tangent. The sheer inappropriateness of critiquing the Academy during a zombie attack is very Always Sunny. Mac's film opinions being delivered with casual expertise he doesn't have is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That can't possibly be what Batman's about. It's about a grown man who dresses up like a bat?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: These are Academy Award winning movies. This is serious stuff.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Well, to bring it all back around, I think when Dee drank the bat blood, that's how she got sick.' / Frank: 'Yes, but the bat juices.' / 'The bat saliva, bat rabies.' / 'Bat rabies, I buy.'
jokes.setup: The Batman debate winds down and they return to their scientific theory about Dee
jokes.punchline: 'Bat rabies, I buy' — Frank endorsing 'bat rabies' as a sensible scientific explanation, as if this is the most credible theory available, is a great deadpan callback to the bat-sucking scene
jokes.explanation: Good callback that closes the loop on the bat-sucking scene. 'Bat rabies, I buy' as Frank's considered scientific verdict is funny in context. The escalating specificity of 'bat juices,' 'bat saliva,' 'bat rabies' is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, you know the Academy, Charlie, I mean...

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I know the Academy as well as anybody. Sometimes, it's atrocious.

jokes.text: Bill Ponderosa: 'Here, have a sip, right from the cow's titty. You'll love it.'
jokes.setup: Bill offers Dee a drink at the wedding
jokes.punchline: 'Right from the cow's titty' — an inexplicably vulgar way to describe what turns out to be spiked milk
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle wedding is a dry milk wedding — so offering it 'from the cow's titty' is both disgusting and contextually appropriate. Rewatch bonus because we now know the milk is spiked with bath salts.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I did something bad. I did something really, really bad; guys, we got to get out of here before everybody finds out what happened.

jokes.text: Bill: 'Come on, it'll loosen you up a bit, make your butthole hot.'
jokes.setup: Dee asks how drinking milk would loosen her up
jokes.punchline: Bill's selling point is that it will 'make your butthole hot' — a specific and disturbing sensation he's describing
jokes.explanation: 'Make your butthole hot' as a drug selling point is specific enough to be genuinely funny. The specificity of the sensation rather than the expected 'it'll make you feel great' is what elevates it. High quotability — this kind of unexpected vulgar specificity sticks.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Here, have a sip, right from the cow's titty. You'll love it.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: How is drinking a glass of milk going to loosen me up, Bill?

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: Well, I spiked the milk with methylenedioxypyrovalerone.

jokes.text: Bill reveals the milk is spiked with 'methylenedioxypyrovalerone' — 'It's bath salts. Yeah, it's like coke and acid and meth all combined. It's awesome.'
jokes.setup: Dee has been drinking mysterious spiked milk at a weird wedding
jokes.punchline: The reveal: it's bath salts — the drug famous for making people eat each other's faces — explaining all the 'zombie' behavior
jokes.explanation: The structural reveal of the entire episode. Bath salts (which were in the news at this time for causing face-eating incidents) explain the zombie behavior perfectly. The whole episode's horror movie premise resolves as a drug-fueled disaster. Bill's casual 'It's awesome' as a summary of a drug that makes people eat faces is perfectly on-brand. High impact because it's the episode's big reveal. Rewatch bonus for all the zombie setup that now makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Bill
dialogue.line: It's bath salts. Yeah, yeah, it's like coke and acid and meth all combined. It's awesome.

jokes.text: Detective: 'Bath salts? The drug that makes people eat each other's faces?'
jokes.setup: The gang explains bath salts caused the zombie behavior
jokes.punchline: The detective's summary — 'the drug that makes people eat each other's faces' — delivered flatly as a matter of public record
jokes.explanation: The detective's flat summary of bath salts' cultural reputation ('the drug that makes people eat each other's faces') as bureaucratic shorthand is very funny. Good economy and deadpan delivery implied.

dialogue.line: Well, I spiked the milk with methylenedioxypyrovalerone. What? It's bath salts. Yeah, yeah, it's like coke and acid and meth all combined.

jokes.text: Gang: 'That is not why I went nuts on you guys.' / 'Huh?' / 'I went nuts on you because of what you assholes did to my goddamn car!'
jokes.setup: Everyone assumes Dee's erratic behavior was from bath salts
jokes.punchline: Dee clarifies: she wasn't acting crazy because of drugs — she was genuinely enraged because they destroyed her car
jokes.explanation: Great misdirection payoff. The gang had a tidy explanation (bath salts) and Dee deflates it — she was genuinely, sanely furious about her car. The idea that her 'crazy' behavior was actually just reasonable anger is a great character note for Dee. Leads perfectly into the car flashback.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, when was the last time you drove a car?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't worry about it, man. I can drive; I remember how.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What happened, dude?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I forgot how to drive.

jokes.text: Charlie drives Dee's car: 'Dude, when was the last time you drove a car?' / Charlie: 'Don't worry about it man, I can drive; I remember how.' / [Immediately crashes]
jokes.setup: Mac asks Charlie when he last drove, Charlie says he 'remembers how'
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately forgets how to drive and crashes, then admits 'I forgot how to drive'
jokes.explanation: Perfectly constructed comedy of overconfidence. 'I remember how' followed immediately by the crash, then 'I forgot how to drive' as the post-crash admission is a great three-beat structure. Very Charlie-specific — his unfounded confidence in skills he doesn't have. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dude, when was the last time you drove a car?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't worry about it, man. I can drive; I remember how.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What happened, dude?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Dude, when was the last time you drove a car?' / 'Don't worry about it, man. I can drive; I remember how.' Then immediately crashes it.
jokes.setup: Charlie is apparently at the wheel of Dee's car
jokes.punchline: 'I remember how' — immediately followed by a crash. His confidence and his actual ability are maximally mismatched
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie confidence-vs.-competence structure. 'I remember how' as the last words before catastrophic failure is perfectly timed. Charlie's vague relationship to practical skills ('I remember how to drive' implying he barely learned once) is very character-specific. The addition of 'I forgot how to drive' as the post-crash assessment is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You sons of bitches! You're gonna pay! You're all gonna pay! I'll kill you!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, we won't pay. We never do.

jokes.text: Post-crash Charlie: 'What happened, dude? What happened?' / 'I forgot how to drive.'
jokes.setup: Charlie just crashed Dee's car
jokes.punchline: 'I forgot how to drive' — delivered as a sincere explanation, as if forgetting is a normal thing that happens mid-drive
jokes.explanation: 'I forgot how to drive' as the entire explanation for a car crash is a great button on the previous joke. The economy is perfect — four words complete the bit. Charlie's flat sincerity makes it land: he's not embarrassed, just reporting the fact of his forgetting.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: Since you're the one with motive and the last one to be seen with her, you're my new #1 suspect.

jokes.text: Dee: 'You sons of bitches! You're gonna pay! You're all gonna pay! I'll kill you! You assholes, you'll pay!' / Mac: 'No, we won't pay. We never do.'
jokes.setup: Dee is screaming threats at the gang who destroyed her car and left her stranded
jokes.punchline: Mac's calm, almost philosophical 'No, we won't pay. We never do.' — both literally true and a meta-commentary on the show's premise
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and arguably the series' thesis statement. 'No, we won't pay. We never do.' works on multiple levels: (1) literally true — they always escape consequences, (2) meta-commentary on the show's premise of terrible people avoiding accountability, (3) delivered with eerie calm that suggests Mac has fully internalized this worldview. Perfect economy — five words that say everything about the show. Very high quotability. Rewatch bonus because this line reads differently with knowledge of the whole series.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: God, Maureen. That was terrible. Who did those tits? The nipple placement is crazy.

jokes.text: Gang attempts to wrap up the story: 'Ba-da-bing.' / Detective: 'Whoa. Sit down, slick.'
jokes.setup: The gang thinks they've explained everything and tries to leave
jokes.punchline: The detective stops them with 'Sit down, slick' — they haven't actually cleared themselves
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat with mild humor. 'Sit down, slick' is a decent detective line. The gang's premature victory is a standard sitcom beat but works fine here.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: Never. Let's run away together.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm gonna run away, but not with you.

jokes.text: Flashback: Dennis visits Maureen. She professes love. Dennis tries to get signature. Maureen: 'Never. Let's run away together.'
jokes.setup: Dennis went to get Maureen's signature on divorce papers at her wedding
jokes.punchline: Instead of signing, Maureen declares she still loves him and wants to run away — the opposite of what Dennis needed
jokes.explanation: Good ironic reversal — Dennis's attempt to finalize the divorce ends with his ex-wife more in love than ever. His entire plan has backfired completely. Standard sitcom comeuppance but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Detective
dialogue.line: You expect me to believe this woman's gonna throw her entire life away just to sleep with her ex-husband on her wedding night? Really?

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Oh, shit. Oh, God, Maureen. That was terrible. Who did those tits? The nipple placement is crazy.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has apparently just had sex with Maureen on her wedding day — which he was trying to prevent
jokes.punchline: His post-coital review focuses entirely on critiquing the surgery's nipple placement
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis character moment and callback. His post-sex commentary — which isn't about Maureen's feelings or the colossal mistake he's made, but purely a consumer review of her plastic surgery — is peak Dennis sociopathy. 'The nipple placement is crazy' as the specific complaint is very funny and very specific. The callback to his earlier 'You big, giant new titties, Maureen!' gives it additional resonance. Character integration is nearly perfect — this thought could only occur to Dennis Reynolds.

dialogue.speaker: Maureen
dialogue.line: Come on, silly head. Let's go home and put this whole adventure behind us.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. No! No, you got to help me. What have I done?

jokes.text: Gang in the interrogation room: 'So all that shit about us ruining the wedding... It turns out you blew it yourself.' / 'Yeah, congratulations, Frank. You win. I'm gonna be paying alimony to that crazy bitch for the rest of my life.'
jokes.setup: Everyone tried to control the wedding outcome; Dennis spent the whole episode trying to get the divorce finalized
jokes.punchline: Dennis ruined his own plan by sleeping with Maureen, who now won't sign anything — Frank's victory declaration is Dennis's permanent defeat
jokes.explanation: Solid episode-closing irony. Dennis's obsession with controlling the outcome (and his inability to control himself around Maureen) is the engine of the whole plot. 'You blew it yourself' is a good gang-on-Dennis burn.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm gonna be paying alimony to that crazy bitch for the rest of my life.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's entire plan for the episode was to end alimony payments
jokes.punchline: He has achieved the perfect opposite — he's now trapped paying alimony forever because he couldn't resist sleeping with Maureen
jokes.explanation: The closing payoff on Dennis's alimony arc is satisfying structurally. His calling Maureen a 'crazy bitch' while himself having made the disastrous choice is properly ironic — his self-awareness is zero.

jokes.text: Detective: 'You expect me to believe this woman's gonna throw her entire life away just to sleep with her ex-husband on her wedding night? Huh? Really? Mr. Reynolds, you're free to go.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just confessed to sleeping with the missing bride on her wedding night
jokes.punchline: The detective finds this so implausible he immediately dismisses Dennis as a suspect and lets him go
jokes.explanation: Great structure — the detective's incredulity that the truth is so absurd it couldn't be a confession. Dennis literally confesses and is released because the story is too ridiculous to believe. The detective's 'Huh? Really?' captures his disbelief perfectly. High earned score because the joke is built on the entire episode's setup.

jokes.text: Maureen appears to bail Dennis out: 'Come on, silly head. Let's go home and put this whole adventure behind us.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been declared free to go
jokes.punchline: Maureen has bailed him out — the worst possible outcome — and addresses him with 'silly head' as though they're a couple again
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button. 'Silly head' as Maureen's term of endearment for Dennis after ruining her wedding, paying his bail, and effectively trapping him forever is an excellent character-specific punchline. Dennis's horror ('No! No! No!') as the final joke closes the loop perfectly. The episode ends worse for Dennis than it began.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'No! No! No, you got to help me. What have I done? You got to help me! What have I done? No! No! No!'
jokes.setup: Maureen has bailed Dennis out and is taking him home as her de facto partner
jokes.punchline: Dennis's complete breakdown — screaming for help from police in an interrogation room, begging to stay arrested
jokes.explanation: Strong closing beat. Dennis preferring prison to going home with Maureen is a great dark punchline. His screaming 'What have I done?' echoing from earlier in the episode ties the whole thing together. Good escalation of despair.

tmdb_overview: The gang make a disturbing discovery after crashing Maureen's wedding.
